results.question: how long do i keep tax records
results.answer:
You must hold on to your tax‑related documents until the IRS can still enforce a tax claim or make a tax assessment, and for any employment‑tax or asset‑related matters that may still be relevant.

**General income‑tax returns**  
* Keep the records that support each item of income or deduction until the “period of limitations” for that return expires.  The period of limitations is the time the IRS can still assess or amend the return.  (See the table of limits in Segment 1.)  Keep copies of the filed tax returns themselves; they help you prepare future returns and prove the amounts you reported.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

**Employment‑tax records**  
* Keep all employment‑tax records for **at least 4 years** after the date the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

**Asset‑related records**  
* Keep records that relate to property (e.g., purchase price, depreciation, improvements, sale details) until the period of limitations expires for the year in which you dispose of that property.  You must keep the records for the *original* property as well as for a new property acquired in a non‑taxable exchange until the disposal year’s limitations period expires.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

**Other non‑tax purposes**  
* When the records are no longer needed for tax purposes, do not discard them until you verify whether any other authority (e.g., creditors, insurance companies) requires a longer retention period.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

These rules cover the primary retention periods required for federal tax records and for employment and property documentation.

results.question: why do i need to keep business records
results.answer:
You need to keep business records for several concrete reasons, all of which are required or recommended by the IRS and other regulators:

1. **They back up the numbers you report on tax returns.**  
   * “These documents contain information you need to record in your books… support the entries in your books and on your tax return.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)  
   * “Support items reported on tax returns. You must keep your business records available at all times for inspection by the IRS.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

2. **They let you prove deductions and credits.**  
   * “It is important to keep these documents because they support the entries… and the credits you report.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)  
   * “Keep records to verify certain information… to figure the annual depreciation and the gain or loss when you sell the assets.” [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13)

3. **They help you monitor and manage the business.**  
   * “Good records can increase the likelihood of business success. Records can show whether your business is improving, which items are selling, or what changes you need to make.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  
   * “You need good records to monitor the progress of your business… prepare your financial statements.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

4. **They satisfy legal and regulatory retention requirements.**  
   * “You must keep your records as long as they may be needed for the administration of any provision of the Internal Revenue Code… the period of limitations for that return runs out.” [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  
   * “Keep copies of your filed tax returns. They help in preparing future tax returns…” [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

5. **They support audits and inspections.**  
   * “A complete set of records will speed up the examination.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  
   * “You must keep your business records available at all times for inspection by the IRS.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

6. **They are necessary for payroll, employment, and other business‑specific filings.**  
   * “If you have employees, you must keep all employment tax records for at least 4 years…” [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13)  
   * “You must keep records to verify certain information about your business assets… to figure the depreciation and the gain or loss when you sell the assets.” [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13)

In short, keeping records is required to satisfy tax law, to protect your right to deductions, to help you run and grow your business, and to meet other legal obligations such as payroll and employment‑tax reporting.

results.question: what accounting method should i use
results.answer:
Your choice of accounting method (cash, accrual, or a combination) depends on a few key facts about your business. Below is a quick decision‑grid that the IRS gives you, followed by the main rules that apply for each choice.

| Question | What it tells you | IRS guidance |
|----------|------------------|--------------|
| **Do you keep inventory that you sell?** | If you need to track inventory, you *must* use the accrual method for sales and purchases of that inventory [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5). | “If an inventory is necessary to account for your income, you must generally use an accrual method of accounting for purchases and sales” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14). |
| **Is your business a small business?** | Small businesses (average annual gross receipts of ≤ $31 million over the past 3 years) may *choose* the cash method even if they hold inventory, as long as they treat inventory as non‑incidental materials or supplies [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16). | “Certain small business taxpayers can use the cash method of accounting and can also account for inventoriable items as materials and supplies” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16). |
| **Do you want simpler bookkeeping?** | The cash method records income when you receive it and expenses when you pay them. It’s usually easier for sole proprietors with no inventory [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16). | “Most individuals and many sole proprietors with no inventory use the cash method” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14). |
| **Do you want to report income in the year it’s earned, not when paid?** | The accrual method matches income and expenses to the period they occur. It’s required for most businesses that sell goods or use inventory [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16). | “Under an accrual method, you generally report income in the tax year you earn it…you deduct or capitalize expenses in the tax year you incur them” [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5). |
| **Do you have special items that need special treatment?** | You can combine methods (e.g., accrual for inventory, cash for other income) if it clearly shows income, but the inventory portion must still use accrual unless you’re a small business exempting it [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5). | “You can generally use any combination of cash, accrual, and special methods…If an inventory is necessary…you must generally use an accrual method for purchases and sales” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5). |

### How to decide
1. **Inventory?**  
   * Yes → use accrual for inventory items.  
   * No → cash is usually fine.  
2. **Small business exemption?**  
   * Yes and inventory is *non‑incidental material* → cash still works.  
3. **Complexity vs. accuracy?**  
   * Prefer simplicity → cash.  
   * Want precise matching of income & expenses → accrual.  

### Practical example
| Scenario | Suggested method | Why |
|----------|------------------|-----|
| Sole proprietor selling handmade crafts, no stock, no employees | Cash | “Most individuals and many sole proprietors with no inventory use the cash method” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14). |
| Store that keeps a ledger of goods to sell (e.g., a boutique) | Accrual | “If an inventory is necessary to account for your income, you must generally use an accrual method” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16). |
| Small coffee shop with modest inventory you consider “non‑incidental” | Cash (if you treat inventory as supplies) | “Certain small business taxpayers can use the cash method…inventory as material or supplies” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16). |

### Changing methods later
If you later decide to switch, you must file Form 3115 for a change in accounting method and usually get IRS approval unless you qualify for an automatic change [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=17)[[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=28).

**Bottom line:**  
*If you don’t keep inventory, pick cash.*  
*If you keep inventory, pick accrual (unless you’re a small business that can treat inventory as non‑incidental supplies, in which case cash is allowed).*  
*If you’re unsure, consider whether you want to match income/expenses to the correct year (accrual) or keep it simple (cash).*

All of the above guidance comes from the IRS publications and sections quoted above.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 14)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)
2. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 16)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)
3. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 5)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)
4. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 17)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=17)
5. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 28)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=28)

results.question: how do i check my workplace for hazards
results.answer:
To check your workplace for hazards, follow the steps recommended in the Small Business Safety and Health Handbook:

1. **Establish a routine self‑inspection program**  
   • Have knowledgeable and experienced workers conduct regular inspections of all work areas.  
   • Use the handbook’s self‑inspection checklists as a starting point. These checklists are based on OSHA standards and general safety principles.  
   • Remember that the checklists are a tool for hazard identification, not a compliance audit. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

2. **Identify, control, and monitor hazards**  
   • For each inspection, note any hazard that is present, decide on a control measure (engineering, administrative, or PPE), and ensure the control is implemented.  
   • After control measures are in place, continue to monitor them to verify they remain effective.  
   • Record your findings in the inspection log and link them to any existing injury/illness data or maintenance logs to spot patterns. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

3. **Use a systematic safety and health program**  
   • Build the self‑inspection activity into a broader safety program that includes:
     – Management leadership and worker participation  
     – Hazard identification and assessment  
     – Hazard prevention and control  
     – Training and communication  
     – Ongoing program evaluation  
   • Regular inspections are highlighted as an “important tool for identifying hazards and fixing them.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7)

4. **Review relevant OSHA standards**  
   • Cross‑check the hazards you find against the applicable portion of OSHA (general industry, construction, etc.) so you know whether the standard already covers the hazard or if a general‑duty issue may exist.  
   • If unsure, call a nearby OSHA Compliance Assistance Specialist or the OSHA On‑Site Consultation Program for free, confidential guidance. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=91)

5. **Keep records and act on findings**  
   • Store inspection records, hazard control plans, and any corrective actions taken.  
   • Update the safety program as new hazards are identified or as work processes change.

In short, perform routine inspections with the handbook checklists, document findings, control identified hazards, and embed this process in a broader safety program—using OSHA resources for clarification when needed.



**Sources:**

results.question: cash or accrual accounting whats the difference
results.answer:
Cash‑method accounting and accrual‑method accounting differ in **when** you record income and expenses on your tax return.

* **Cash method** – You count income only in the year you actually receive it, and you deduct (or capitalize) expenses in the year you actually pay them.  
* **Accrual method** – You count income in the year you earn it, even if the payment comes later, and you deduct or capitalize expenses in the year you incur them, even if you haven’t paid them yet.

These rules are the core distinction between the two methods[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5).



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 5)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

results.question: can i deduct business travel
results.answer:
Yes, you can deduct ordinary and necessary expenses that are incurred while you are traveling away from your regular place of business.  The IRS allows you to take a deduction for:

* **Transportation** – the cost of flying, taking a train, bus, or driving a car between your home (or regular workplace) and the temporary work site. You may use the actual cost or the standard mileage rate (70¢ per business‑use mile in 2025).  Tolls and parking that are directly related to the trip are also deductible.  Baggage and shipment of samples to the temporary site can be deducted.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)

* **Meals** – you may deduct the cost of meals while away from home for an overnight or longer business trip.  Generally only 50 % of the meal expense is deductible, unless you elect the standard meal allowance under Pub. 463.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)

* **Lodging** – full deduction for the cost of hotel or other overnight lodging that is required for the trip.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)

* **Telephone and communication** – business calls made while traveling, including fax and other communication devices, are deductible.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)

* **Tips** – tips paid for any of the above travel expenses are deductible.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)

* **Other incidental business expenses** – dry‑cleaning, laundry, and other necessary travel costs may be deducted.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)

**Recordkeeping** – keep receipts and a written record of the purpose of the trip, the business relationship with the people you visit, and the date and duration of the travel.  These records are required to substantiate the deduction.  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

In short, expenses that are ordinary, necessary, and directly related to your business travel—transportation, meals (50 %), lodging, communication, tips, and incidental travel costs—are deductible.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 41)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)
2. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 11)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

results.question: what goes in an executive summary
results.answer:
An executive summary is the first concise snapshot of the entire business plan.  According to the guide, it should be one or two short paragraphs that give the reader an overview of what the business seeks to accomplish.  It typically includes:

* **The core idea or product/service** that the business will offer.  
* **How much money is needed** and what the capital will be used for (equipment, marketing, working‑capital, etc.).  
* **How much money the owners have already invested** (equity) or plan to bring in.  
* A **brief timeline or schedule of key milestones** and goals.

The summary is intentionally brief, is best written after the rest of the plan is complete, and serves to hook the reader into the rest of the document.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)



**Sources:**
1. [sba_business_planning_guide.pdf (Page 4)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)

results.question: how do i describe my target market
results.answer:
To describe your target market you need to paint a clear, concise picture of the customers you want to reach and attract.  The business‑plan guidance gives a step‑by‑step framework:

1. **Define the market niche** – state the specific segment of the market that your product or service best serves.  
   *Example: “Our niche is health‑conscious college students living in urban campuses.”* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

2. **Identify who your best customers are** – list “ideal” buyer profiles.  
   *Example: “Female, 18–24, full‑time students, income $10–15 k a year, lives in university housing.”* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

3. **Describe key characteristics** – describe the demographics (age, gender, income), psychographics (values, lifestyle, attitudes), geographic location, and behavioral traits (purchase frequency, brand loyalty).  
   *Example: “They value convenience, are tech‑savvy, and prefer eco‑friendly products.”* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

4. **Segment the market** – choose a segmentation basis that fits the product:  
   * *Business markets*: industry, company size, location, product use.  
   * *Consumer markets*: age, gender, income, lifestyle, benefits sought.  
   *Example: “We segment students by campus location and by interest in organic foods.”* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

5. **Estimate size and growth** – use data (population, sales, industry reports) to project how large the chosen segment is and its expected growth. Mention the percentage of the total market you anticipate capturing.  
   *Example: “The student population in our 5‑city area is ~200 k, growing 3 % annually; we aim to capture 5 % of this segment.”* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

6. **Justify why this segment matters** – explain the fit between your product/service and the segment’s needs, and how your offering meets a specific benefit or solves a problem.  
   *Example: “Our plant‑based protein bars satisfy the demand for quick, healthy snacks among active students.”* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

By following those steps you create a focused, data‑backed target‑market description that will guide your marketing strategy and reassure investors that you understand who you are selling to.



**Sources:**
1. [sba_business_planning_guide.pdf (Page 14)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

results.question: do i have to make my shop wheelchair accessible
results.answer:
Yes.  
Because your shop is a private business that serves the public, it is considered a **public accommodation** under the ADA. The law requires such businesses, regardless of size, to remove any “readily achievable” physical barriers that prevent people who use wheelchairs from entering and moving about the premises. The ADA does not exempt existing facilities from these duties, and “readily achievable” means any reasonable or inexpensive modification that can be made by your business’s size and resources.  

**Key requirements that apply to a shop**

| Issue | ADA requirement (excerpt) | Source |
|-------|--------------------------|--------|
| **Accessible entrance** – at least one entrance must be usable by a wheelchair, or an alternative accessible entrance with a signed way must be provided | “If one entrance is not accessible and another entrance is accessible, a sign must provide direction to the accessible entrance…the alternative entrance must be open during store hours” | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10) |
| **Doors** – must be at least 36 in. clear width and use accessible hardware (lever, flat‑panel) | “Doors that are less than 36 in. need to be widened or fitted with ‘swing‑clear’ hinges…door hardware that requires a tight grasp must be replaced by a lever or loop handle” | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12) |
| **Clear interior route** – a 36‑in. wide pathway to the sales area, with a minimum 3‑ft turning space at corners | “A 36 in. wide accessible route is needed…provide a 3‑ft by 3‑ft turning space at a corner for a 90° turn” | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) |
| **Parking** – at least one accessible parking space per 25 public‑parking spaces, and the spaces must be close to an accessible entrance with a sign | “If your parking lot has 25 or fewer spaces, then 1 should be an accessible parking space…must be located on level ground and within an accessible route” | [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8) |
| **Counters and service areas** – a lowered section at or below 36 in. high, with 30" × 48" free space in front | “An accessible sales counter at least 36 in. long and no more than 36 in. above the floor…a 30 in. by 48 in. clear floor space in front” | [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15) |

If any of these elements are not “readily achievable” (for example, the cost or effort is too great), the ADA allows you to defer removal, but you must still provide the good or service through an alternative method such as delivery, alternative service lines, or a home‑delivery system.

results.question: am i exempt from injury recordkeeping
results.answer:
The publication explains the circumstances in which an employer is **partially exempt** from OSHA’s injury‑and‑illness recordkeeping rules:

* If the employer had **10 or fewer employees during every month of the previous calendar year** you may be exempt from keeping the required OSHA Form 300 log, Form 301 incident reports, and the Form 300A yearly summary. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)  
* If the employer is in a **low‑hazard industry** listed in 29 CFR 1904, Subpart B, Appendix A, you may likewise be exempt. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)

All employers—regardless of size or industry—**must still report** work‑related fatalities, in‑patient hospitalizations, amputations, and loss of an eye to OSHA. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)

You would need to check those facts against the rules above. If you have 10 or fewer employees all year and your industry is listed as low‑hazard in 29 CFR 1904.1 or Appendix A, you would be exempt; otherwise you are not. | What to keep | How long (OSHA rule) | Source |
|--------------|----------------------|--------|
| OSHA **Form 300** (Log of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses) | **5 years** from the end of the calendar year covered | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |

results.question: how do i start a business and keep my taxes organized
results.answer:
**Starting a business and keeping its taxes in order**

1. **Pick a legal structure**  
   • Sole proprietorship, partnership, LLC, C‑corp, or S‑corp.  
   • The structure determines the tax return you file and the taxes you owe.  
   – Sole proprietor → Form 1040 + Schedule C (and, if self‑employed, Schedule SE) [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=6)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11).  
   – Partnership → Form 1065; each partner reports income on 1040 + Schedule E [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=6)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11).  
   – C‑corp → Form 1120 [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=6)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11).  
   – S‑corp → Form 1120‑S (and Schedule SE for owners) [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=6)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11).  
   – LLC → tax treatment is chosen by the owner(s); choose “disregarded entity,” partnership, C‑corp, or S‑corp.  

2. **Get an Employer Identification Number (EIN)** – the IRS tax ID for your business.  
   – You need an EIN if you have employees, file excise tax, or choose to use it instead of your SSN.  
   – Apply online at IRS.gov/EIN; no cost.  
   – You will receive a PIN package that enrolls you automatically in EFTPS for federal tax deposits.  
   – Obtain any necessary “payee identification numbers” (See Segment 13).  

3. **Adopt a tax year**  
   – Most new businesses use a calendar year (1 Jan–31 Dec).  
   – If you start later, you can choose a fiscal year, but you must file Form 1128 to change it later and may pay a user fee.  
   – The tax year you file with on your first business return becomes your schedule.  

4. **Pick an accounting method** – cash or accrual (or a specialty method).  
   – Cash method: record income when received, expenses when paid.  
   – Accrual method: record income when earned and expenses when incurred.  
   – You choose when you file your first business return.  
   – Changing the method later requires IRS approval (see Pub. 538).  

5. **Open a separate business bank account** and use a business checking account for all business money.  
   – Keep all receipts, invoices, bank statements, and check stubs.  
   – Reconcile your book balance with the bank statement each month.  

6. **Keep the required records**  
   – Maintain a complete, separate set of books for each business.  
   – Record every income and expense, keeping supporting documents (receipts, invoices, bank deposits).  
   – Electronic records are acceptable if they meet the IRS retention and access requirements.  
   – Keep records for the period of limitations: 3 years for ordinary income and most deductions, 7 years for higher‑income taxpayers, and 4 years for employment‑tax records [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)[[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14).  

7. **File the right forms and pay on time**  
   | Tax | Form(s) | Due dates | Notes | [Citation] |
   |------|--------|-----------|-------|-------------|
   | Income (earned as a sole proprietor, partner, or S‑corp shareholder) | 1040 S, 1040‑SE | 15 Oct next year (or due date of tax return) | Pay by 15 Oct if $1 000+ self‑employment tax is owed | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11) |
   | Corporate income (C‑corp) | 1120 | 15 Apr next year | Over‑payment by 30 days is due (no extension) | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11) |

results.question: do i need an ein and what accounting method comes with it
results.answer:
**Do you need an EIN?**  
- An *Employer Identification Number (EIN)* is required if you:  
   • pay wages to one or more employees, or  
   • file pension or excise‑tax returns, or  
   • want a separate business tax identification number rather than using your Social‑Security # 【Segment 4】.  
- If you are a sole proprietor with **no employees** and have no other reason listed above, you can use your SSN for tax reporting, although many choose to obtain an EIN anyway for bank accounts and business‑related activities 【Segment 4】.  

**Which accounting method “comes with” an EIN?**  
- An EIN itself does **not** determine a specific accounting method.  
- When you file your first income‑tax return for the business (e.g., Schedule C for a sole proprietor), you must choose an accounting method that will be used for all future returns unless IRS approval is obtained to change it.  
- You can choose either the **cash method** or the **accrual method**:   
   • **Cash method** – income is reported when cash is actually received; expenses are deducted when paid 【Segment 5】.  
   • **Accrual method** – income is reported when earned, even if cash is received later; expenses are deducted when incurred 【Segment 5】.  
- If your business keeps an inventory, the IRS generally requires you to use the accrual method for purchases and sales, though small‑business taxpayers may elect a simplified treatment 【Segment 24】.  

**Summary**  
- Get an EIN if you meet the criteria above; otherwise you may use your SSN.  
- When you first file taxes, choose either the cash or accrual method; the choice is independent of whether you have an EIN.

**Retention periods for tax records (as officially required by the IRS)**  

| Type of record | Required retention period | Source |
|----------------|--------------------------|--------|
| 1. General income‑tax return receipts, supporting documents, and copies of filed returns | Keep until the “period of limitations” for that return expires.  For most returns that means **3 years** from the date the return was filed.  If you under‑reported income by 25 % or more, it is **6 years**; if you filed a fraudulent return it is **not limited**. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| 2. Employment‑tax records (e.g., payroll, tax withholding, Forms 941/944, etc.) | Keep for **at least 4 years** after the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| 3. Recordkeeping for property/assets | Keep records relating to a property until the period of limitations expires for the year in which you **dispose of the property in a taxable disposition**. These records are needed to compute depreciation, amortization, and basis for gain/loss calculations. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| 4. Copies of all filed returns | Keep them because they help prepare future returns and support any amended return. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| 5. Non‑tax‑related records (e.g., insurance, creditor documents)| Do not discard until you confirm that any required non‑tax retention period has passed; these may extend the duration beyond the IRS requirement. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |

**Key points**

* The “period of limitations” is the timeframe in which you can amend a return or the IRS can assess additional tax.  
* For most individuals and businesses, that period is **3 years** from the return’s filing date.  
* For certain situations (large under‑reporting, fraud, or specific types of returns) the period can be longer.  
* Employment‑tax records have a separate rule: at least **4 years** from the due/pay date.  
* Asset‑related records must endure until the limitation period of the year you sell or otherwise dispose of the asset.  

These are the specific retention obligations for federal tax records as documented in the IRS guidance.

runs.question: what accounting method should i use
runs.answer:
The IRS requires you to pick one “accounting method” when you file your first income‑tax return for the business, and you must keep that method (or a consistent combination of methods) going forward unless you get IRS approval to change it.  The choice depends mainly on whether you keep inventory and how complex your bookkeeping needs to be.

**1. Cash method** – If you are a sole proprietor who does **not keep inventory** (or for whom inventory can be treated as non‑incidental materials or supplies), the cash method is usually the simplest and most common choice.  
- You record income in the year you actually receive or are constructively received the payment.  
- Expenses are deducted in the year you pay them.  
- The cash method is “easier to keep records” for most individuals and sole proprietors without inventory. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)

**2. Accrual method** – Use the accrual method if you **keep inventory** that must be valued and reported, or if you need to match income with the expenses that produced it.  
- Income is reported when earned (the all‑events test is met).  
- Expenses are deducted or capitalized when incurred, regardless of when they are paid.  
- “If an inventory is necessary to account for your income, you must generally use an accrual method of accounting for sales and purchases.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)  
- Even small businesses that keep inventory can use the cash method **only if** they treat the inventory as non‑incidental materials or supplies; otherwise accrual is required. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)

**3. Combination or special methods** –  
- You may mix cash, accrual, and special methods for different items, as long as the combination “clearly shows your income.”  
- If you use a combination that includes the cash method, the combination is treated as cash.  
- Certain small‑business taxpayers can also use special methods for items such as bad debts, depreciation, or sales of inventory. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)

**5. Selecting the method you’ll use** – In practice, most new sole‑proprietors who do not keep inventory choose the cash method because it matches the times they actually receive income and pay expenses, and it requires fewer record‑keeping rules. If you expect to hold inventory or your business model calls for matching income and expenses (e.g., a manufacturer or retailer), start with the accrual method or the small‑business accrual‑for‑inventory exception. Keep separate books and records for each business and maintain the chosen method unless you file for a change. runs.question: how do i check my workplace for hazards
runs.answer:
To find and fix hazards in your workplace you can follow the self‑inspection approach that the handbook recommends:

1. **Start with a systematic self‑inspection**  
   * Have knowledgeable workers (or a safety team) repeatedly walk through every part of the work area and look for anything that could cause injury or illness.  
   * Use the handbook’s *Self‑Inspection Checklists* – they cover the major categories that apply to general‑industry workplaces (not construction or maritime).  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)  

2. **Document what you see**  
   * Record each potential hazard, the condition that makes it dangerous, and any control that is already in place.  
   * Note whether the control is effective – do the workers still see the hazard? Is the control kept up to date?  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)  

3. **Cross‑reference with records and training**  
   * Combine the checklist findings with your injury/illness logs, maintenance records, and worker training schedules. This will help you spot patterns that you might miss during a single walk‑through.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)  

4. **Use OSHA resources for guidance**  
   * After you’ve identified hazards, consult the OSHA website or call your local **On‑Site Consultation Program** (free, confidential). The program can help you determine what standards apply and how to control the hazards.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)  

5. **Apply the “Hazard Identification and Assessment” element of OSHA’s recommended safety and health program**  
   * The handbook’s “Implementing a Safety and Health Program” section outlines a step‑by‑step plan that covers hazard identification, prevention, and control.  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7)  

6. **Repeat the process regularly**  
   * Hazards can appear when equipment changes, new chemicals are introduced, or work practices evolve.  Schedule inspections at least quarterly, or whenever major changes occur.  [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=9)  

7. **Record findings and actions**  
   * Keep a log of each inspection, the hazards found, and the actions taken. Share this log with workers so they see that the workplace is improving.  [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=9)  

By routinely inspecting, documenting, and consulting the OSHA tools described above, you can systematically detect hazards, evaluate whether existing controls are working, and implement new controls to keep the workplace safe.

runs.question: cash or accrual accounting whats the difference
runs.answer:
Cash vs. accrual accounting means **when** you count income and expenses on your tax return.

| Feature | Cash method | Accrual method |
|--------|-------------|----------------|
| **Income** | Report income when you actually receive it (or when it becomes constructively available). | Report income when you earn it—i.e., when the right to receive the payment is fixed, even if you haven’t yet got the money. |
| **Expenses** | Deduct (or capitalize) an expense in the year you actually pay it, unless the expense is paid in advance; then you deduct it in the year it applies. | Deduct or capitalize an expense in the year it is incurred—when liability is fixed and economic performance has occurred. |
| **Inventory** | Most cash‑method users who keep inventory must use an inventory system that is consistent with the cash method, or qualify as a small business to treat inventory as non‑incidental supplies. | If you keep inventory, you almost always must use an accrual method for purchases and sales, because inventory is part of the business’s income‑generating activity. |
| **Recording** | Simpler; matches real cash flow, good for small businesses that don’t keep inventory. | Matches income and expenses in the same year, giving a clearer picture of profitability for businesses that sell goods or provide services on credit. |
| **Example (income)** | You receive a $1,000 check on December 30 2024 but don’t deposit it until January 2 2025. Under cash you report the $1,000 in 2025. | You deliver a product in December 2025, invoice the customer in January 2026, and receive payment in February 2026. Under accrual you still report the $1,000 in 2025 because the income was earned then. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5) |
| **Example (expense)** | You pay $500 for office supplies in January 2026 that were bought in December 2025. Under cash you deduct the $500 in 2026. | You buy supplies in December 2025, incur the expense that month, and pay in January 2026. Under accrual you deduct the expense in 2025. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5) |

### Why choose one over the other?
- **Cash** is easier and often meets IRS requirements for many small, non‑inventory‑based businesses.  
- **Accrual** provides a more accurate picture of financial health, especially for businesses that sell on credit or keep inventory, and it is required when inventory is involved.  

If you keep inventory, you must use an accrual method for that inventory, even if you otherwise use cash for other items (unless you qualify as a small business that can treat inventory as supplies). [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)  

In short, **cash accounting matches the actual receipt and payment of money, whereas accrual accounting matches the earning and incurring of money, regardless of when cash changes hands.**

runs.question: how do i describe my target market
runs.answer:
To describe your target market you should follow the steps outlined in the business‑planning guide:

1. **Identify the niche and the best customer** – State the specific group of people or businesses that your product or service is designed for.  
   *Example:* “Our niche is eco‑friendly kitchen gadget creators who want to reduce waste.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

2. **Define customer characteristics** – Describe who these customers are along dimensions that matter to your business, such as:  
   - **Demographics** (age, gender, income, education)  
   - **Geographic location** (city, region, country)  
   - **Psychographics** (lifestyle, values, interests)  
   - **Behavioral traits** (purchase frequency, brand loyalty, product usage)  
   *These elements help you paint a clear picture of the “typical” buyer.”* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

3. **Segment the market** – If you sell to more than one type of customer, split the overall market into segments (e.g., consumer vs. business, small‑scale vs. mass‑market). Then indicate which segment(s) you will target first. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

4. **Estimate market size and growth potential** – Use data such as population figures, industry reports, or sales‑tax information to calculate:  
   - Total addressable market (TAM)  
   - Serviceable available market (SAM)  
   - Share you aim to capture (e.g., “We expect to capture 5 % of the SAM within three years.”) [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

5. **Connect the target market to your business strategy** – Explain how the chosen characteristics align with your product, price, promotion, and distribution strategies. This shows why the market is a good fit for your business plan. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

By following these steps you provide a clear, data‑backed picture of who you are selling to and why they will buy from you, which is the core of a strong target‑market description.

runs.question: do i have to make my shop wheelchair accessible
runs.answer:
Yes.  
The Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) requires any private business that serves the public to make its premises accessible to people who use wheelchairs (or other mobility devices) unless a barrier is **not “readily achievable”** to correct.

- **Coverage:** “Private businesses that provide goods or services to the public are covered by the ADA and must remove physical barriers that are readily achievable” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6).  
- **Existing facilities:** Existing facilities built before 1993 are not exempt; they must still remove such barriers. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)  
- **Requirements:** If an accessible entrance or route is impossible to create, the business must provide alternative service (e.g., home delivery) or at least an accessible entrance that is “readily achievable” (steps removed or replaced with a ramp, turn‑slope ≤ 1:12, handrails, 36‑in. wide pathway, etc.) [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15).  

So, if you own or operate a shop that the public can visit, you are legally required to make it wheelchair‑accessible or remove the barrier in a way that is readily achievable.

runs.question: am i exempt from injury recordkeeping
runs.answer:
Yes. The OSHA record‑keeping requirements give a **partial exemption** under two specific conditions, but they do not eliminate all reporting obligations.  

* **Partial exemption if you meet one of the following**  
  * Had **10 or fewer workers** during **every month** of the previous calendar year – see 29 CFR 1904.1.  
  * Operate in a **low‑hazard industry** as defined in 29 CFR 1904, Subpart B, Appendix A.  

  These employers are **not required** to keep OSHA Forms 300, 301, or 300A for ordinary recordable injuries or illnesses.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)  

* **What you must still do**  
  * **All employers**—regardless of size or industry—must **report** any work‑related **fatality, inpatient hospitalization, amputation, or loss of an eye** to OSHA.  
  * If you **do have** recordable injuries/illnesses (even if you’re exempt from routine recordkeeping) you must still keep a **supplementary record** on OSHA Form 301 and hold that record for at least five years.  
  * If your establishment has **250 or more workers** or **20–249 workers** in certain high‑hazard industries, you must electronically submit an **annual summary** (OSHA Form 300A) by **March 2** of the next calendar year.  

  These requirements apply even to exempt employers if they fall into those size or industry categories.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)  

So, if your business had ≤10 workers last year **or** is in a low‑hazard industry, you are **partially exempt** from routine recordkeeping, but still must report major injuries/fatalities and keep backup records if any injury occurs.

[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| **Employment‑tax records** (payroll reports, Forms 941/944, wage‑statement records, W‑2, W‑3, payroll journals). | They are needed to verify payroll deductions and employer tax payments. | At least **4 years after the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later**. | **Electronic records** – if you keep a computer‑based system that stores the same books and records as a hard‑copy system, you must keep that system “as long as it is **material to the administration of tax law**.” | The IRS can test your electronic system; it must be able to reproduce and provide the same data as the hard‑copy books. | The same retention period as the hard‑copy records it replaces – i.e., until the limitation period for the related return or other tax purpose expires. Employment‑tax documents get a minimum of 4 years, and asset‑related documents survive as long as the year in which the asset is disposed of.

   Decide whether your business will be a sole proprietorship, partnership, limited‑liability company (LLC), or corporation (C‑ or S‑).  The legal form determines the tax return you must file, the type of taxes you owe and whether you can have employees [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=3).  

2. **Register the business name**  
   If you use a name that is not your own last name (or that differs from your corporation’s legal name), file a “fictitious name” or “doing‑business‑as” (DBA) statement with the Secretary of State or the county Register of Deeds [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=6).  

3. **Obtain an Employer Identification Number (EIN)**  
   An EIN is required if you have employees, pay excise tax, or simply want a business‑specific tax ID instead of using your SSN.  Apply online through the IRS at www.irs.gov/ein [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=6).  

4. **Pick a tax year**  
   • Calendar year (Jan 1 – Dec 31) is the default if you keep no books, have no annual accounting period, or the law requires it.  
   • Fiscal year is any 12‑month period ending on the last day of a month other than December.  
   File Form 1128 if you need to change the tax year later [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5).  

5. **Select an accounting method**  
   • **Cash method**: record income when received and expenses when paid.  
   • **Accrual method**: record income when earned and expenses when incurred.  
   Choose the method when you file your first income‑tax return with the business schedule [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11)[[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14).  

6. **Set up a record‑keeping system**  
   *Open a dedicated business checking account and keep a business checkbook.*  Record all receipts, bank deposits, payroll, and expenses, and reconcile the account each month [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14).  
   *Maintain supporting documents* (sales slips, invoices, deposit slips, canceled checks) and store them either on paper or in an electronic system that can be audited by the IRS [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12).  
   *Use a single‑entry or double‑entry bookkeeping system* depending on complexity; in either case, keep a summary of cash receipts, a check‑disbursements journal, and a payroll record [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15).  

7. **Track business expenses and deductions**  
   Deduct ordinary and necessary expenses (housing, travel, car, startup costs up to $5,000, depreciation).  Keep detailed records of each expense to support the deduction [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=9)[[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)[[11]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11).  

8. **File required tax returns**  
   • Sole proprietor: Form 1040 with Schedule C (and Schedule SE if self‑employment tax applies).  
   • Partnership: Form 1065.  
   • C‑corp: Form 1120.  
   • S‑corp: Form 1120‑S.

runs.answer:
**Keep Employees Safe**

| Action | What the segment says | Citations |
|--------|------------------------|-----------|
| **Keep walkways clean, stable, and free of hazards** | Walking‑working surfaces must be kept clean, orderly, and sanitary; wet surfaces must be covered, drainage maintained, and false floors or mats provided. Holes and debris must be repaired or covered. Plastic and other material must not project into walkways. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=78) |
| **Maintain machinery and equipment** | All machinery must be clean, properly maintained, and have sufficient clearance. Each machine must have a power‑shut‑off switch within reach of the operator, emergency‑stop buttons colored red, lock‑out for hazardous energy, and splash guards for coolant‑used machines. | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=54) |
| **Provide fall protection & guardrails** | Guardrails on aisles or walkways above four feet (1.2 m) must be installed. Walkways should allow adequate headroom and be inspected regularly. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=78)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=79) |
| **Emergency action plan & training** | A written emergency plan must identify evacuation conditions, a clear chain of command, evacuation routes, and procedures for people with disabilities. Workers must be trained on the plan and on what to do in an emergency. | [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=26)[[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=28) |
| **Lockout/Tag‑out** | Machinery must be locked out before servicing; stored energy must be released or blocked, and only exposed workers may place or remove locks. | [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=50)[[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=18) |
| **Electrical safety** | Ensure all electrical equipment is grounded, cords inspected, and workers trained in CPR. Do not work alone on energized lines over 600 V. | [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=18)[[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=17) |
| **Portable ladder safety** | Ladders must be in good condition, secured on slippery surfaces, and always extend at least 3 ft above the work surface. Workers must keep three points of contact. | [[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=75) |
| **Maintain aisles and exit paths** | Exits must be unobstructed, clearly signed, and have two means of egress where needed. Exit signs must be at least 6 inches above ground. | [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=28)[[11]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=23) |
| **Workplace violence prevention** | Have a written program, training on de‑escalation, and engineering controls (panic buttons, alarms). Keep records of incidents and conduct workplace violence risk assessments. | [[12]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=85)[[13]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=86)[[14]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=84) |

**Keep Your Premises Accessible**

| Requirement | Specified Parameters | Citations |
|-------------|----------------------|-----------|
| **Accessible entrance** | Entrance must be no higher than 2 ft, no steps (or ramps with a slope ≤ 1:12). A ramp requires handrails on either side, a landing at least 18 in wide and 60 in beyond the door, slope 1:12, and width ≥ 32 in. If an alternate entrance exists, clearly signpost to it; the alternate must be open during business hours. | [[15]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)[[16]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11) |
| **Turnstiles / security gates** | Turnstiles must be removed or altered to provide a clear opening of at least 32 in; if a turnstile remains, an accessible gate must be installed. | [[17]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=13)[[18]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12) |
| **Door hardware** | Doors ≥ 36 in wide are preferred; old doors < 36 in can be widened or fitted with “swing‑clear” hinges. Handle types that require a tight grasp, such as round knobs or thumb latches, must be replaced by lever or loop handles. | [[18]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12) |
| **Ramps, edge protection & handrails** | Ramp slope max 1:12, width ≥ 36 in, handrails on both sides, edge protection to prevent rolling. | [[16]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11) |
| **Parking** | At least one accessible parking space for every ≤ 25 total spaces, and a second for ≤ 50. Accessible parking spaces must be at least 8 ft wide, have an access aisle 5 ft (car) or 8 ft (van) wide, be level, and marked with the international symbol. Provide a vertical clearance of ≥ 98 in. | [[19]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8)[[20]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=9) |
| **Accessible route within building** | A continuous, wide (≥ 36 in) route from entrance to all sales or service areas. Where aisles are narrower, widen them or provide staff assistance. | [[21]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) |
| **Sales and service counters** | At least 36 in long, ≤ 36 in above floor; provide 30×48 in floor space in front of the counter for a wheelchair. If not possible, provide a lowered section or auxiliary counter. | [[22]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15) |
| **Serving counters in restaurants** | If counter height > 34 in, provide a lowered section at least 60 in long and no higher than 34 in. | [[23]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16) |
| **Fixed seating & tables** | Table height 28–34 in; knee clearance ≥ 27 in; clear floor space 30×48 in. 5 % (or at least one if < 20) of tables in a dining area must be accessible. | [[24]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=17) |
| **Accessible paths & turn spaces** | Provide a 36‑in wide accessible route and 60‑in diameter turning space for 180° turns; at corners give extra space. | [[21]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) |
| **Bilingual/communication** | Use labels for customers with visual or hearing impairments; consider TDD relay and sign‑language interpreters for complex transactions. | [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=18) |
| **Seating & dining** | Accessible seating must be available in any food service area; the seat height must be ≤ 34 in. | [[24]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=17) |

runs.question: how do i write a business plan and set up accounting
runs.answer:
**Answer**

Below is a step‑by‑step guide that pulls directly from the provided segments.  
Each piece of information is tied to the segment(s) in which it appears – “[Segment N]” is the citation.  
If a part of the question is not covered by any segment, that portion is noted as *INSUFFICIENT*.

---

## 1. Writing a Business Plan  

| Section | Key Content | Source |
|--------|-------------|--------|
| **Cover Page** | Name, address, phone, owners’ details, logo, date | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4) |
| **Table of Contents** | Optional but useful for navigation | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4) |
| **Executive Summary** | 1–2 paragraphs summarizing idea, funding needs, use of funds, and timeline | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4) |
| **Business Description** | Overview of the product/service, unique value, regulations, facilities, equipment | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12) |
| **Market Analysis** | Total market, target market, competition, barriers, marketing strategy | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12), [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) |
| **Management & Organization** | Ownership structure, key personnel, responsibilities, external consultants | [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=13) |
| **Operations Plan** | Daily operations, supply chain, inventory, quality control | [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=5), [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12), [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=15) |
| **Financial Plan** | Sources & uses, 3‑year income projection, cash‑flow, balance sheet, break‑even analysis, notes & assumptions | [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=16) |
| **Appendices / Exhibits** | Resumes, contracts, leases, credit reports, floor plans | [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=17) |
| **Checklist for SBDC / SCORE Review** | Verify figures, assumptions, and legal structure | [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=5) |

**How to start**

1. **Collect information** – Use the “Checklist for Purchasing a Business” in [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=5) to structure data collection, even if you’re not purchasing.
2. **Draft the plan** – Write each major section in the order listed. Most firms write the *Executive Summary* last, but the outline in [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4) suggests writing it last as well.  
3. **Prepare financials** – Create a Sources & Uses worksheet, 3‑year projections, cash‑flow schedule, and balance sheet (see [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=16) for formats and guidance).  
4. **Add supporting documents** – Attach all exhibits mentioned in [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=17).  
5. **Review with mentors** – Consider SBDC or SCORE help ([[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=3), [[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=53)).  

---

## 2. Setting Up Accounting  

| What to Do | How to Do It | Source |
|------------|--------------|--------|

runs.question: do i need an ein and what accounting method comes with it
runs.answer:
**Do you need an EIN?**  
*  **If you have employees, if you file pension or excise‑tax returns, or if you want a separate business tax ID for other purposes, the IRS requires that you obtain an Employer Identification Number (EIN).**  
   * “EINs are assigned to sole proprietors, LLCs, corporations, and other entities by the IRS…you must also include your EIN on all returns…[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=4)”*  
*  **If you are a sole‑proprietor with no employees and you are not filing pension or excise‑tax returns, you can use your Social‑Security number (SSN) as the taxpayer identification number (TIN) and an EIN is optional.**  
   * “…If you…have an EIN, include it on Schedule C…(Form 1040)…[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)”*  

**What accounting method is “with” an EIN?**  
*An EIN does not dictate an accounting method. When you file your first income‑tax return for the business you choose an accounting method—cash or accrual (or, for some specific items, a combination).**  
   * “Choosing an Accounting Method…You choose an accounting method for your business when you file your first income‑tax return that includes a Schedule C (Form 1040). After that, if you want to change your accounting method, you must generally get IRS approval…[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)”*  

In short: get an EIN if you meet the criteria above; the accounting method you use is chosen independently when you file your first return.

runs.question: what forms do i keep for injuries and how long do i keep them
runs.answer:
**Forms you must keep for injuries**

| OSHA form | Description | When you file it |
|-----------|-------------|------------------|
| **OSHA Form 300** – *Log of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses* | A daily record of every work‑related injury or illness that is recordable under OSHA (e.g., medical treatment beyond first aid, amputation, eye loss). | Filled out at the time of the injury/illness and kept as part of the ongoing log. |
| **OSHA Form 301** – *Injury and Illness Incident Report* | A detailed incident report for each recordable case identified on the Form 300. | Prepared and filed after the injury/illness is documented on Form 300. |
| **OSHA Form 300A** – *Summary of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses* | An annual summary of the company’s recordable injuries and illnesses, used for reporting to OSHA and internal monitoring. | Filed each calendar year on or before March 2 of the following year (for employers that must submit it, such as those with 250+ workers). |

**How long to keep them**

All the OSHA injury and illness records—Forms 300, 301, and 300A—must be retained **at the worksite for at least five (5) years** after the date of the injury or illness.  
[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) provides the five‑year retention requirement.  
[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14) lists the specific forms that must be kept as part of OSHA’s injury and illness recordkeeping system.

runs.question: how long do i keep tax records
runs.answer:
To know how long to keep your tax‑related papers, look to the IRS “period of limitation” rules that apply to each type of record.

**Income and deduction records** – Keep every document that supports an item of income or a deduction on a return until the period of limitation for that return expires. The default periods are:

- **3 years** from the date the return was filed (or the due date if filed early).  
- **6 years** if you report income that is more than 25 % of the gross income shown.  
- **7 years** if the return is fraudulent.  
- **Not limited** if the return is filed after a late‑filed extension or if you claim a credit for a tax period not covered by the above limits. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

**Employment‑tax records** – If you hire employees, keep all employment‑tax records for **4 years** after the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

**Asset–related records** – Keep documents that describe property you own (depreciation, amortization, basis calculations) until the period of limitation for the year in which you dispose of that property. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

**Other notes**

- Keep copies of every filed tax return; they are needed for future returns or amended returns.  
- If records are no longer needed for tax purposes, don’t discard them right away—some other agencies (insurance, creditors) may require them longer than the IRS does.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)
