runs.question: why do i need to keep business records
runs.answer:
You need to keep business records because they are the backbone of both your tax compliance and your day‑to‑day business operations.

1. **Support your tax returns** – The IRS requires you to keep documents that prove your income, deductions, and credits.  Supporting documents such as sales slips, receipts, invoices, deposit slips, and canceled checks are needed to back up the numbers you report on your return.  The records must be available in case the IRS audits you.  “It is important to keep these documents because they support the entries in your books and on your tax return.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)

2. **Provide evidence in case of an IRS examination** – If the IRS inspects your returns, they may ask you to explain the items reported.  A complete set of records will speed up the examination and reduce the chance of penalties.  “You must keep your business records available at all times for inspection by the IRS.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

3. **Monitor the progress of your business** – Good records let you see whether your business is improving, which items are selling, or what changes you need to make.  “Records can show whether your business is improving, which items are selling, or what changes you need to make.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

4. **Prepare accurate financial statements** – Income (profit and loss) statements and balance sheets are built from the same records you use for taxes.  These statements are essential when dealing with banks, creditors, or investors.  “You need good records to prepare accurate financial statements. These statements can help you in dealing with your bank or creditors and help you manage your business.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

5. **Maintain required legal and tax records** – Some records, such as corporate minutes or employee tax documents, are required by law to be kept for a specified period.  “You must keep the records on the old property, as well as on the new property, until the period of limitations expires.” [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

In short, keeping thorough, organized records lets you comply with tax law, defend yourself if the IRS questions you, and manage your business more effectively.

runs.question: what accounting method should i use
runs.answer:
If you are just starting a sole‑proprietor business, you can pick the method that best matches your actual book‑keeping habits and the type of inventory you carry:

| Situation | Suggested method | Why it fits | Source |
|-----------|------------------|------------|--------|
| **No inventory or only very small, non‑incidental supplies** | **Cash method** – record income when you receive money and expenses when you pay them. | It is the simplest way for many sole proprietors to keep accurate records, and the IRS allows it unless you need an inventory system. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=54) |
| **Inventory is required to track sales** | **Accrual method** – record sales when you earn them and expenses when you incur them, even if you don’t yet receive the cash. | The accrual method is designed to match revenue and related costs in the same period, which is essential when products are stored or shipped. | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=54) |
| **You fit the IRS definition of a “small business taxpayer”** (average annual gross receipts of **$31 million or less** for the previous three tax years, indexed for inflation) and you have inventory | You can **continue with the cash method** and treat inventory as material supplies that are not incidental, as long as your inventory accounting still “clearly reflects your income.” | Small businesses are granted flexibility to use cash for purchases and sales if the inventory treatment is consistent with reporting income. | [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16) |
| **You need to change your chosen method later** | File Form 3115, Application for Change in Accounting Method. | IRS approval is required for a change of accounting method. | [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=17) |

**How to choose**

1. **File your first return** with the method you intend to use. That becomes your tax‑year basis for that year.  
2. **Keep books consistent** – the same method must be used for calculating taxable income and for your record‑keeping.  
3. **Re‑evaluate if inventory or business volume changes.** If you start holding inventory after beginning on cash, you will need to switch to accrual (unless you qualify as a small business and choose the special small‑business exception).  
4. **Seek IRS approval** if you decide to switch to a different method for any reason other than the small‑business exception.

In summary:  
*Use the cash method if you have no inventory (or only very small, non‑incidental supplies).  
Use the accrual method if you need to keep inventory, unless you qualify as a small business and prefer the small‑business exception that allows cash for inventory.*

runs.question: how do i check my workplace for hazards
runs.answer:
To check your workplace for hazards, follow the steps and tools outlined in the handbook:

1. **Start with a self‑inspection**  
   • Designate experienced, knowledgeable workers to conduct routine safety and health inspections (self‑inspections).  
   • Use the handbook’s *Self‑Inspection Checklists* as a starting point. These checklists cover general‑industry areas and help you spot hazards before they cause injury.  
   • After each checklist, review the linked resources for deeper guidance on specific hazards. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

2. **Document and analyze the findings**  
   • Record checklist results, injury/illness logs, training records, maintenance logs, and any incident reports.  
   • Combine this data to identify patterns and pinpoint where control measures are lacking.  
   • Use OSHA standards and other resources listed in the handbook to find solutions.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

3. **Use a safety and health program framework**  
   • Develop a safety and health program that includes management leadership, worker participation, systematic hazard identification, and control.  
   • Schedule regular inspections; involve workers in reporting and solving hazards.  
   • Keep a written procedure for workers to report injuries, illnesses, incidents, hazards, and concerns.  
   • Ensure continuous training on hazard identification and control. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=9)

4. **Check specific hazard areas**  
   * **Ergonomics** – assess for heavy lifting, repetitive motions, awkward postures, and use the ergonomics checklist to prioritize controls. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=21)  
   * **Hazard communication/chemicals** – inventory hazardous chemicals, keep Safety Data Sheets (SDS) up to date, label containers, and train workers on SDS and labeling. [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=38)  
   * **Walkways** – keep walking surfaces clean, repair holes, provide non‑slip materials, and maintain adequate headroom and guardrails. [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=79)  
   * **Confined spaces** – identify and evaluate permit‑required confined spaces, post danger signs, secure inspections, and perform atmospheric tests. [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=66)  
   * **Workplace violence** – evaluate risk factors, establish a prevention program, review training (de‑escalation, emergency response). [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=84)  
   * **Heat‑related illness** – train workers on heat hazards, signs, first aid, and ensure proper hydration and rest breaks. [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=44)  

5. **Leverage OSHA resources**  
   • Consider a **consultation visit** from OSHA’s On‑Site Consultation Program (no‑cost, confidential). A consultant can help you assess hazards and improve controls.  
   • Use OSHA tools: safety‑program self‑evaluation, implementation checklists, and audit tools.  
   • If your state has an OSHA‑approved State Plan, review its specific requirements.  
   [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=90)

6. **Maintain records and continuously improve**  
   • Keep accurate records of inspections, hazard controls, incidents, and training.  
   • Review the program annually, update procedures, and adjust controls as needed.  
   • Use the safety‑program evaluation tool to track progress and set new goals.  
   [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=9)

By following these steps—regular self‑inspections, thorough documentation, targeted hazard checks, worker involvement, and using OSHA’s support resources—you can systematically identify and control workplace hazards, keeping your employees safe.

runs.question: can i deduct business travel
runs.answer:
Yes – if the travel is **ordinary and necessary** for your trade or business you can deduct the related expenses on your tax return.  
The deductions include:

* **Transportation** – airfare, train, bus, or car mileage (actual costs or the standard mileage rate).  You may also deduct business‑related tolls, parking fees, and, if you use the standard mileage rate, the interest on a car loan and certain state/local taxes.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=35)  
* **Lodging** – hotels or other overnight accommodations required while away from your “tax home.”  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)  
* **Meals** – 50 % of the cost can be deducted (you may elect the standard meal allowance).  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)  
* **Telephone, fax, and other communication costs** while traveling.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)  
* **Tips, cleaning, and laundry** incurred during the trip.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)  
* **Reimbursement of employees** – expenses you reimburse under an accountable or non‑accountable plan are deductible (outside the scope of a personal deduction). [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)  

The trip must meet the IRS definition of traveling **away from home**: the duties require you to be away from your regular work area for longer than an ordinary day’s work and you need sleep or rest to perform your work.  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)  

All these costs can be taken on Schedule C (Form 1040) for sole proprietors or the appropriate business form for other entities.  No specific filing deadline for the deduction itself exists beyond the normal tax‑year deadlines; the deduction is reported when you file your annual return. - A very short section (usually one or two paragraphs).  
- It gives the reader a quick snapshot of the business plan.

  - How much money you need and what you will use it for.  
  - How much money you already have invested (or will bring in).  
  - A short timeline or schedule of your major goals.

runs.question: how do i describe my target market
runs.answer:
To describe your target market you should follow the steps outlined in the business‑plan guide:

1. **Define the market niche and the best customer** – Identify who your product or service appeals to the most.  
   * “Describe your market niche; who is your best customer. Identify those customers and describe their characteristics.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

2. **Segment the market** – Decide how to group potential buyers.  
   * Consumer markets can be segmented by demographics (age, gender), geographic location, economic status, lifestyle, or by the product benefits they seek.  
   * Business markets can be segmented by industry, company size, location, or product use/application. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

   * “Estimate the approximate size and growth potential of the target market(s) using population figures, sales tax info, industry information, etc.”  
   * “Estimate how much of the total market you will capture.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

4. **Support with data** – Use industry reports, demographic data, and any available sales or tax statistics to back your estimates.

5. **Tie it to your marketing strategy** – In your plan, explain how the target‑market description informs your product, service, and promotional choices.

runs.question: do i have to make my shop wheelchair accessible
runs.answer:
Yes – as a private business that serves the public you are covered by the ADA and must remove physical barriers that are **“readily achievable.”** The law does not require you to make the entire shop fully wheelchair‑accessible, but it does require you to eliminate barriers that can be removed without unreasonable difficulty or expense.  

**Key points from the guidance**

* **All private businesses that provide goods or services to the public are public accommodations** and must comply with ADA Title III. Any barrier that is “readily achievable” must be removed [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6).  
* The ADA gives a lower bar for existing facilities built before 1993 (or altered before 1992). Even so, you still must remove barriers that are easily improvable and consider the business’s resources [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=5).  
* “Readily achievable” is judged on the size, resources and type of your business. For small shops this usually means:
  * **Accessible entrance(s)** – remove steps, provide a ramp or lift, or offer an alternative accessible entrance [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12)[[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11).  
  * **Accessible parking** – provide the required number of accessible spaces and use an access aisle of at least 5 ft for cars (or 8 ft for vans) [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=9).  
  * **Accessible service counters/pages** – a lowered section of at least 36 in. high, with a clear 30 × 48‑in. maneuvering space [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15)[[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16).  
  * **Narrow doorways or hardware** – widen doors to at least 36 in. clear width and replace knobs with lever or loop handles [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12).  
  * **Aisles and shelves** – keep at least 36 in. wide between displays and shelves for wheelchair circulation [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14).  

If any of these improvements would be *unreasonable* for your shop (very extreme cost, structural limitations, etc.), you may justify that they are not “readily achievable,” but you still must address barriers that can be fixed economically and without major remodeling.  

In short: **you are required to remove barriers that you can do reasonably.** If you can’t make the entire shop fully accessible, you must at least make it reasonably accessible to people using wheelchairs. This may involve ramps, accessible counters, accessible parking, and accessible entrances, among other measures.

runs.question: am i exempt from injury recordkeeping
runs.answer:
You may be partially exempt from OSHA’s injury‑and‑illness record‑keeping rules if one of the following applies to your business – but remember you still must report certain serious incidents (fatalities, hospitalizations, amputations, and loss of an eye) to OSHA at any size:

* **Fewer than 10 employees during the entire last calendar year** – this is the “10‑worker” exemption.  
* **Your industry is listed as “low‑hazard”** in **29 CFR 1904, Subpart B, Appendix A** – this is the “low‑hazard” exemption.  

If you meet either of those conditions you are NOT required to keep OSHA Form 300 logs, Form 301 incident reports, or Form 300A summaries, though you must still report the types of incidents mentioned above within the required time frames [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14). If you do not meet those conditions, you must comply with the full record‑keeping and reporting requirements.

[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| Employment‑tax records (payroll reports, Forms 941/944, W‑2s, W‑3s, etc.). | At least **4 years** after the date the tax became due or was paid, whichever is later. | Records that are no longer needed for tax but might be required for insurance, creditors, or other non‑tax purposes. | Do not discard until you verify those other parties have no longer required them. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |

**Injury / OSHA records**

| Record | Retention requirement |
|--------|------------------------|
| OSHA Form 300 (Log of work‑related injuries and illnesses) | Keep at the worksite for **at least five (5) years**. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| OSHA Form 300A (Annual Summary of work‑related injuries and illnesses) | Same five‑year requirement. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| OSHA Form 301 (Injury and Illness Incident Report) | Keep each recordable case form for **5 years**. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| Worker medical and exposure records | Retain for the period required for each specific type of record (often 7 – 10 years, depending on the injury or illness). [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| Worker training records | Keep accessible to workers and for the duration of the training program; OSHA requires these be available for review. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| Records of fatalities, in‑patient hospitalizations, amputations, or loss of an eye | Must be reported to OSHA within 8, 24, and 24 hours respectively, and retained per the OSHA recording rules. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| General OSHA compliance records (e.g., injury logs, incident reports) | Must be available for OSHA’s inspection and retained as required by OSHA regulations, typically **5 years** for injury/illness logs. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14) |

**Key take‑away**

- For tax, keep supporting documents and payroll records for the same time the tax return is required (usually 3–6 years) and employment‑tax records for at least 4 years.  
- For injuries, keeping OSHA Forms 300, 300A, and 301, plus related medical, exposure, and training records, is required for **five (5) years**.  

Both sets of records help protect you in case of an IRS audit or an OSHA inspection and ensure you have the necessary documentation if you need to amend a return or rebut an employer‑safety claim.

runs.question: what do i need to do to keep employees safe and my premises accessible
runs.answer:
**What you need to do to keep employees safe *and* make your premises accessible**

---

### 1. Walk‑working surfaces, aisles and general housekeeping  
*Clean, dry and unobstructed paths are the first line of safety.*  
- Keep walkways free of spills, obstructions and “holes”.  Repair or cover any defects at the earliest opportunity.  Wet surfaces must be covered with non‑slip material or, where possible, drainage must be maintained.  All walking surfaces must be inspected regularly and maintained in a safe condition [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=78)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=79).  
- Ensure a minimum 36‑inch wide aisle throughout the store so people—including those in wheelchairs—can turn and pass easily.  Provide a 36‑inch clear path at 90‑degree turns, and a 60‑inch diameter circle for 180‑degree turns [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14).  
- If walkways run near moving machinery or welding operations, arrange them so workers are not exposed to hazards.  
- Provide adequate headroom (at least 4 ft = 48 in) and guardrails on any raised surface [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=78).  

### 2. Machinery & equipment safety  
*Equip–and‑secure* the machines that your staff use.  
- Keep all machines clean and regularly maintained.  Provide a power‑shutdown switch within reach of the operator and lock‑out/tag‑out (LO/TO) devices for any hazardous energy when servicing.  Only the exposed worker may place or remove the lock.  Make sure the machine is a complete lock‑out from the main power source, not just a push‑button [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=54)[[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=50)[[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=49).  
- Fit splash guards, guard‑rails, emergency‑stop buttons (colored red) and eye‑safety screens.  Ensure clearances around machines for safe operation, servicing and material handling [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=54)[[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=73).  
- Train all operators and maintain a written LO/TO procedure that is reviewed at least annually [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=50)[[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=49).

### 3. Emergency action & evacuation plans  
*Know what to do before a crisis occurs.*  
- Draft an emergency action plan that identifies the types of emergencies, the chain of command, evacuation routes and roles for all employees (including those with disabilities).  The plan must specify how injured workers, visitors and non‑English speakers are assisted.  Post the plan in a prominent location.  Review it annually [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=26)[[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=27)[[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=25).  
- Mark exit routes with illuminated exit signs (letters at least 6 in tall, ¾‑in width) and ensure they are free of obstruction.  At least two means of egress are required from dangerous areas, and each exit must open from the direction of exit traffic without keys or special knowledge [[11]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=28)[[12]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=23).  
- Keep emergency telephone numbers posted where they can be found immediately [[13]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=13).

### 4. Accessible entrance and interior routes  
*Everyone should be able to get in, move around and leave the premises.*  
- The first entrance must be accessible: a ramp or lift whose slope is no steeper than 1:12 (for a 6‑in rise, 72‑in run), handrails when the rise exceeds 6 in, and edge‑protection.  The opening at an entrance must be at least 32 in wide; if a turnstile is present, remove it or replace it with an accessible gate

**How to write a business plan**  
1. **Cover Page & Table of Contents** – list company name, address, phone, owners and dates.  
2. **Executive Summary** – a one‑to‑two‑paragraph snapshot of the idea, money needed, use of funds, and projected timeline.  
3. **Business Description** – explain the product or service, industry, and competitive edge.  
4. **Marketing Plan** – detail target market, competition, pricing, promotion, and distribution.  
5. **Management & Operations** – outline structure, key roles, staffing, suppliers, and facilities.  
6. **Financial Section** – include:  

   * Sources & Uses of Funds statement  
   * Three‑year income projection (monthly)  
   * Cash‑flow projection (three years)  
   * Balance sheet (at a fixed date)  
   * Break‑even analysis  
   * Notes & critical assumptions for the projections  

   These documents demonstrate the feasibility of the venture and are required by lenders.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=16)  

7. **Exhibits** – attach deeds, leases, contracts, resumes, and any other evidence that supports the plan.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)

### Quick checklist for the first year

1. **Create the business plan** – use the outline above.  
2. **Register the business name** – file a fictitious name with the county or Secretary of State if required.  
3. **Obtain an EIN** – no fee, online.  
4. **Choose a tax year** – calendar year unless you have a special situation.  
5. **Select an accounting method** – cash for most small services; accrual if you keep inventory or are a small business taxpayer who can’t track inventory.  
6. **Open a dedicated business checking account** – keep personal and business funds separate.  
7. **Set up a record‑keeping system** – either single‑entry (cash register + daily recap) or double‑entry (journals & ledgers).  
8. **Collect and file sources & uses statement** – shows where money comes from and where it goes.  
9. **Allocate and document payroll and employee details** – keep a payroll

runs.question: do i need an ein and what accounting method comes with it

**Do you need an EIN?**  
- An EIN is required for businesses that **pay wages to one or more employees** or that **file certain federal excise or pension tax returns** [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6).  
- If your business is a **sole proprietorship, partnership, LLC, or corporation**, the IRS assigns an EIN for tax filing and reporting purposes, even if you don't have employees [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=4).  
- A sole‑prop owner *may* choose to get an EIN instead of using their Social Security number for business tax matters, but it is not mandatory unless one of the above situations applies [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=6).

**What accounting method comes with an EIN?**  
- An EIN **does not determine** the accounting method you must use.  
- The accounting method is chosen separately

runs.question: how long do i keep tax records
runs.answer:
You must hold on to your tax‑related documents until the IRS can still enforce a tax claim or make a tax assessment, and for any employment‑tax or asset‑related matters that may still be relevant.

**General income‑tax returns**  
* Keep the records that support each item of income or deduction until the “period of limitations” for that return expires.  The period of limitations is the time the IRS can still assess or amend the return.  (See the table of limits in Segment 1.)  Keep copies of the filed tax returns themselves; they help you prepare future returns and prove the amounts you reported.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

**Employment‑tax records**  
* Keep all employment‑tax records for **at least 4 years** after the date the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

**Asset‑related records**  
* Keep records that relate to property (e.g., purchase price, depreciation, improvements, sale details) until the period of limitations expires for the year in which you dispose of that property.  You must keep the records for the *original* property as well as for a new property acquired in a non‑taxable exchange until the disposal year’s limitations period expires.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

**Other non‑tax purposes**  
* When the records are no longer needed for tax purposes, do not discard them until you verify whether any other authority (e.g., creditors, insurance companies) requires a longer retention period.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

These rules cover the primary retention periods required for federal tax records and for employment and property documentation.

runs.question: why do i need to keep business records
runs.answer:
You need to keep business records for several concrete reasons, all of which are required or recommended by the IRS and other regulators:

1. **They back up the numbers you report on tax returns.**  
   * “These documents contain information you need to record in your books… support the entries in your books and on your tax return.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)  
   * “Support items reported on tax returns. You must keep your business records available at all times for inspection by the IRS.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

2. **They let you prove deductions and credits.**  
   * “It is important to keep these documents because they support the entries… and the credits you report.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)  
   * “Keep records to verify certain information… to figure the annual depreciation and the gain or loss when you sell the assets.” [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13)

3. **They help you monitor and manage the business.**  
   * “Good records can increase the likelihood of business success. Records can show whether your business is improving, which items are selling, or what changes you need to make.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  
   * “You need good records to monitor the progress of your business… prepare your financial statements.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

4. **They satisfy legal and regulatory retention requirements.**  
   * “You must keep your records as long as they may be needed for the administration of any provision of the Internal Revenue Code… the period of limitations for that return runs out.” [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  
   * “Keep copies of your filed tax returns. They help in preparing future tax returns…” [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

5. **They support audits and inspections.**  
   * “A complete set of records will speed up the examination.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  
   * “You must keep your business records available at all times for inspection by the IRS.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

6. **They are necessary for payroll, employment, and other business‑specific filings.**  
   * “If you have employees, you must keep all employment tax records for at least 4 years…” [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13)  
   * “You must keep records to verify certain information about your business assets… to figure the depreciation and the gain or loss when you sell the assets.” [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13)

In short, keeping records is required to satisfy tax law, to protect your right to deductions, to help you run and grow your business, and to meet other legal obligations such as payroll and employment‑tax reporting.

runs.question: what accounting method should i use
runs.answer:
Your choice of accounting method (cash, accrual, or a combination) depends on a few key facts about your business. Below is a quick decision‑grid that the IRS gives you, followed by the main rules that apply for each choice.

| Question | What it tells you | IRS guidance |
|----------|------------------|--------------|
| **Do you keep inventory that you sell?** | If you need to track inventory, you *must* use the accrual method for sales and purchases of that inventory [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5). | “If an inventory is necessary to account for your income, you must generally use an accrual method of accounting for purchases and sales” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14). |
| **Is your business a small business?** | Small businesses (average annual gross receipts of ≤ $31 million over the past 3 years) may *choose* the cash method even if they hold inventory, as long as they treat inventory as non‑incidental materials or supplies [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16). | “Certain small business taxpayers can use the cash method of accounting and can also account for inventoriable items as materials and supplies” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16). |
| **Do you want simpler bookkeeping?** | The cash method records income when you receive it and expenses when you pay them. It’s usually easier for sole proprietors with no inventory [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16). | “Most individuals and many sole proprietors with no inventory use the cash method” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14). |
| **Do you want to report income in the year it’s earned, not when paid?** | The accrual method matches income and expenses to the period they occur. It’s required for most businesses that sell goods or use inventory [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16). | “Under an accrual method, you generally report income in the tax year you earn it…you deduct or capitalize expenses in the tax year you incur them” [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5). |
| **Do you have special items that need special treatment?** | You can combine methods (e.g., accrual for inventory, cash for other income) if it clearly shows income, but the inventory portion must still use accrual unless you’re a small business exempting it [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5). | “You can generally use any combination of cash, accrual, and special methods…If an inventory is necessary…you must generally use an accrual method for purchases and sales” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5). |

### How to decide
1. **Inventory?**  
   * Yes → use accrual for inventory items.  
   * No → cash is usually fine.  
2. **Small business exemption?**  
   * Yes and inventory is *non‑incidental material* → cash still works.  
3. **Complexity vs. accuracy?**  
   * Prefer simplicity → cash.  
   * Want precise matching of income & expenses → accrual.  

### Practical example
| Scenario | Suggested method | Why |
|----------|------------------|-----|
| Sole proprietor selling handmade crafts, no stock, no employees | Cash | “Most individuals and many sole proprietors with no inventory use the cash method” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14). |
| Store that keeps a ledger of goods to sell (e.g., a boutique) | Accrual | “If an inventory is necessary to account for your income, you must generally use an accrual method” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16). |
| Small coffee shop with modest inventory you consider “non‑incidental” | Cash (if you treat inventory as supplies) | “Certain small business taxpayers can use the cash method…inventory as material or supplies” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16). |

### Changing methods later
If you later decide to switch, you must file Form 3115 for a change in accounting method and usually get IRS approval unless you qualify for an automatic change [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=17)[[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=28).

**Bottom line:**  
*If you don’t keep inventory, pick cash.*  
*If you keep inventory, pick accrual (unless you’re a small business that can treat inventory as non‑incidental supplies, in which case cash is allowed).*  
*If you’re unsure, consider whether you want to match income/expenses to the correct year (accrual) or keep it simple (cash).*

All of the above guidance comes from the IRS publications and sections quoted above.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 14)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)
2. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 16)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)
3. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 5)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)
4. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 17)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=17)
5. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 28)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=28)

runs.question: how do i check my workplace for hazards
runs.answer:
To check your workplace for hazards, follow the steps recommended in the Small Business Safety and Health Handbook:

1. **Establish a routine self‑inspection program**  
   • Have knowledgeable and experienced workers conduct regular inspections of all work areas.  
   • Use the handbook’s self‑inspection checklists as a starting point. These checklists are based on OSHA standards and general safety principles.  
   • Remember that the checklists are a tool for hazard identification, not a compliance audit. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

2. **Identify, control, and monitor hazards**  
   • For each inspection, note any hazard that is present, decide on a control measure (engineering, administrative, or PPE), and ensure the control is implemented.  
   • After control measures are in place, continue to monitor them to verify they remain effective.  
   • Record your findings in the inspection log and link them to any existing injury/illness data or maintenance logs to spot patterns. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

3. **Use a systematic safety and health program**  
   • Build the self‑inspection activity into a broader safety program that includes:
     – Management leadership and worker participation  
     – Hazard identification and assessment  
     – Hazard prevention and control  
     – Training and communication  
     – Ongoing program evaluation  
   • Regular inspections are highlighted as an “important tool for identifying hazards and fixing them.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7)

4. **Review relevant OSHA standards**  
   • Cross‑check the hazards you find against the applicable portion of OSHA (general industry, construction, etc.) so you know whether the standard already covers the hazard or if a general‑duty issue may exist.  
   • If unsure, call a nearby OSHA Compliance Assistance Specialist or the OSHA On‑Site Consultation Program for free, confidential guidance. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=91)

5. **Keep records and act on findings**  
   • Store inspection records, hazard control plans, and any corrective actions taken.  
   • Update the safety program as new hazards are identified or as work processes change.

In short, perform routine inspections with the handbook checklists, document findings, control identified hazards, and embed this process in a broader safety program—using OSHA resources for clarification when needed.

runs.question: cash or accrual accounting whats the difference
runs.answer:
Cash‑method accounting and accrual‑method accounting differ in **when** you record income and expenses on your tax return.

* **Cash method** – You count income only in the year you actually receive it, and you deduct (or capitalize) expenses in the year you actually pay them.  
* **Accrual method** – You count income in the year you earn it, even if the payment comes later, and you deduct or capitalize expenses in the year you incur them, even if you haven’t paid them yet.

These rules are the core distinction between the two methods[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5).

1. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 5)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

runs.question: can i deduct business travel
runs.answer:
Yes, you can deduct ordinary and necessary expenses that are incurred while you are traveling away from your regular place of business.  The IRS allows you to take a deduction for:

* **Transportation** – the cost of flying, taking a train, bus, or driving a car between your home (or regular workplace) and the temporary work site. You may use the actual cost or the standard mileage rate (70¢ per business‑use mile in 2025).  Tolls and parking that are directly related to the trip are also deductible.  Baggage and shipment of samples to the temporary site can be deducted.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)

* **Meals** – you may deduct the cost of meals while away from home for an overnight or longer business trip.  Generally only 50 % of the meal expense is deductible, unless you elect the standard meal allowance under Pub. 463.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)

* **Lodging** – full deduction for the cost of hotel or other overnight lodging that is required for the trip.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)

* **Telephone and communication** – business calls made while traveling, including fax and other communication devices, are deductible.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)

* **Tips** – tips paid for any of the above travel expenses are deductible.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)

* **Other incidental business expenses** – dry‑cleaning, laundry, and other necessary travel costs may be deducted.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)

**Recordkeeping** – keep receipts and a written record of the purpose of the trip, the business relationship with the people you visit, and the date and duration of the travel.  These records are required to substantiate the deduction.  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

In short, expenses that are ordinary, necessary, and directly related to your business travel—transportation, meals (50 %), lodging, communication, tips, and incidental travel costs—are deductible.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 41)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)
2. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 11)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

runs.question: what goes in an executive summary
runs.answer:
An executive summary is the first concise snapshot of the entire business plan.  According to the guide, it should be one or two short paragraphs that give the reader an overview of what the business seeks to accomplish.  It typically includes:

* **The core idea or product/service** that the business will offer.  
* **How much money is needed** and what the capital will be used for (equipment, marketing, working‑capital, etc.).  
* **How much money the owners have already invested** (equity) or plan to bring in.  
* A **brief timeline or schedule of key milestones** and goals.

The summary is intentionally brief, is best written after the rest of the plan is complete, and serves to hook the reader into the rest of the document.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)



**Sources:**

runs.question: how do i describe my target market
runs.answer:
To describe your target market you need to paint a clear, concise picture of the customers you want to reach and attract.  The business‑plan guidance gives a step‑by‑step framework:

1. **Define the market niche** – state the specific segment of the market that your product or service best serves.  
   *Example: “Our niche is health‑conscious college students living in urban campuses.”* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

2. **Identify who your best customers are** – list “ideal” buyer profiles.  
   *Example: “Female, 18–24, full‑time students, income $10–15 k a year, lives in university housing.”* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

3. **Describe key characteristics** – describe the demographics (age, gender, income), psychographics (values, lifestyle, attitudes), geographic location, and behavioral traits (purchase frequency, brand loyalty).  
   *Example: “They value convenience, are tech‑savvy, and prefer eco‑friendly products.”* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

4. **Segment the market** – choose a segmentation basis that fits the product:  
   * *Business markets*: industry, company size, location, product use.  
   * *Consumer markets*: age, gender, income, lifestyle, benefits sought.  
   *Example: “We segment students by campus location and by interest in organic foods.”* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

5. **Estimate size and growth** – use data (population, sales, industry reports) to project how large the chosen segment is and its expected growth. Mention the percentage of the total market you anticipate capturing.  
   *Example: “The student population in our 5‑city area is ~200 k, growing 3 % annually; we aim to capture 5 % of this segment.”* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

6. **Justify why this segment matters** – explain the fit between your product/service and the segment’s needs, and how your offering meets a specific benefit or solves a problem.  
   *Example: “Our plant‑based protein bars satisfy the demand for quick, healthy snacks among active students.”* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

By following those steps you create a focused, data‑backed target‑market description that will guide your marketing strategy and reassure investors that you understand who you are selling to.

runs.question: do i have to make my shop wheelchair accessible
runs.answer:
Yes.  
Because your shop is a private business that serves the public, it is considered a **public accommodation** under the ADA. The law requires such businesses, regardless of size, to remove any “readily achievable” physical barriers that prevent people who use wheelchairs from entering and moving about the premises. The ADA does not exempt existing facilities from these duties, and “readily achievable” means any reasonable or inexpensive modification that can be made by your business’s size and resources.  

**Key requirements that apply to a shop**

| Issue | ADA requirement (excerpt) | Source |
|-------|--------------------------|--------|
| **Accessible entrance** – at least one entrance must be usable by a wheelchair, or an alternative accessible entrance with a signed way must be provided | “If one entrance is not accessible and another entrance is accessible, a sign must provide direction to the accessible entrance…the alternative entrance must be open during store hours” | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10) |
| **Doors** – must be at least 36 in. clear width and use accessible hardware (lever, flat‑panel) | “Doors that are less than 36 in. need to be widened or fitted with ‘swing‑clear’ hinges…door hardware that requires a tight grasp must be replaced by a lever or loop handle” | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12) |
| **Clear interior route** – a 36‑in. wide pathway to the sales area, with a minimum 3‑ft turning space at corners | “A 36 in. wide accessible route is needed…provide a 3‑ft by 3‑ft turning space at a corner for a 90° turn” | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) |
| **Parking** – at least one accessible parking space per 25 public‑parking spaces, and the spaces must be close to an accessible entrance with a sign | “If your parking lot has 25 or fewer spaces, then 1 should be an accessible parking space…must be located on level ground and within an accessible route” | [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8) |
| **Counters and service areas** – a lowered section at or below 36 in. high, with 30" × 48" free space in front | “An accessible sales counter at least 36 in. long and no more than 36 in. above the floor…a 30 in. by 48 in. clear floor space in front” | [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15) |

runs.question: am i exempt from injury recordkeeping
runs.answer:
The publication explains the circumstances in which an employer is **partially exempt** from OSHA’s injury‑and‑illness recordkeeping rules:

* If the employer had **10 or fewer employees during every month of the previous calendar year** you may be exempt from keeping the required OSHA Form 300 log, Form 301 incident reports, and the Form 300A yearly summary. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)  
* If the employer is in a **low‑hazard industry** listed in 29 CFR 1904, Subpart B, Appendix A, you may likewise be exempt. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)

All employers—regardless of size or industry—**must still report** work‑related fatalities, in‑patient hospitalizations, amputations, and loss of an eye to OSHA. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)

You would need to check those facts against the rules above. If you have 10 or fewer employees all year and your industry is listed as low‑hazard in 29 CFR 1904.1 or Appendix A, you would be exempt; otherwise you are not. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)

runs.question: what records do i keep for tax and for injuries and for how long
runs.answer:

| Supporting documents for income and deductions (sales slips, invoices, receipts, bank deposits, canceled checks, etc.) | Same period of limitations as the return they support—or until the IRS requires them for a longer period (e.g., for insurance or creditor purposes) | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| Employment‑tax records (withholding, payroll, FICA, FUTA, etc.) | At least **4 years** after the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| Asset‑related records (purchase, improvements, depreciation, disposition) | Until the period of limitations expires in the year the asset is disposed of in a taxable disposition | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| Records for non‑tax purposes that may later need to be kept longer (e.g., insurance claims, creditor requirements) | Do not discard until you have confirmed no longer needed for those other purposes | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |

*If you use an electronic record‑keeping system, keep it under the same retention guidelines as the paper books, and ensure it can be reproduced in a legible format – with indexing, storage, retrieval, and preservation controls that the IRS would accept.* [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)  

**Injury / illness records (OSHA)**  

| What to keep | How long (OSHA rule) | Source |
|--------------|----------------------|--------|
| OSHA **Form 300** (Log of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses) | **5 years** from the end of the calendar year covered | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| OSHA **Form 301** (Injury and Illness Incident Report) | **5 years** from the end of the calendar year covered | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| OSHA **Form 300A** (Summary of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses) | **5 years** from the end of the calendar year covered | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| Records of first‑aid treatment, worker medical records, training records, exposure records, and any other documents that must be retained for injury/illness investigations | **At least 5 years** for the OSHA injury/illness logs; other records may have industry‑specific or employer‑specific requirements (e.g., 8 hours for fatalities, 24 hours for hospitalizations) | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15), [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14) |

**Key take‑away**

- For tax matters, keep records long enough to cover the IRS’s period of limitations for that return, plus an extra 4 years for employment‑tax documents and a period equal to the asset’s disposition for asset records.  
- For injuries and illnesses, keep OSHA Forms 300, 301, and 300A, plus related reports and medical records, on site and in a legible, secure format for **5 years** from the end of each calendar year they cover.

runs.question: how do i start a business and keep my taxes organized
runs.answer:
**Starting a business and keeping its taxes in order**

1. **Pick a legal structure**  
   • Sole proprietorship, partnership, LLC, C‑corp, or S‑corp.  
   • The structure determines the tax return you file and the taxes you owe.  
   – Sole proprietor → Form 1040 + Schedule C (and, if self‑employed, Schedule SE) [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=6)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11).  
   – Partnership → Form 1065; each partner reports income on 1040 + Schedule E [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=6)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11).  
   – C‑corp → Form 1120 [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=6)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11).  
   – S‑corp → Form 1120‑S (and Schedule SE for owners) [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=6)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11).  
   – LLC → tax treatment is chosen by the owner(s); choose “disregarded entity,” partnership, C‑corp, or S‑corp.  

2. **Get an Employer Identification Number (EIN)** – the IRS tax ID for your business.  
   – You need an EIN if you have employees, file excise tax, or choose to use it instead of your SSN.  
   – Apply online at IRS.gov/EIN; no cost.  
   – You will receive a PIN package that enrolls you automatically in EFTPS for federal tax deposits.  
   – Obtain any necessary “payee identification numbers” (See Segment 13).  

3. **Adopt a tax year**  
   – Most new businesses use a calendar year (1 Jan–31 Dec).  
   – If you start later, you can choose a fiscal year, but you must file Form 1128 to change it later and may pay a user fee.  
   – The tax year you file with on your first business return becomes your schedule.  

4. **Pick an accounting method** – cash or accrual (or a specialty method).  
   – Cash method: record income when received, expenses when paid.  
   – Accrual method: record income when earned and expenses when incurred.  
   – You choose when you file your first business return.  
   – Changing the method later requires IRS approval (see Pub. 538).  

5. **Open a separate business bank account** and use a business checking account for all business money.  
   – Keep all receipts, invoices, bank statements, and check stubs.  
   – Reconcile your book balance with the bank statement each month.  

6. **Keep the required records**  
   – Maintain a complete, separate set of books for each business.  
   – Record every income and expense, keeping supporting documents (receipts, invoices, bank deposits).  
   – Electronic records are acceptable if they meet the IRS retention and access requirements.  
   – Keep records for the period of limitations: 3 years for ordinary income and most deductions, 7 years for higher‑income taxpayers, and 4 years for employment‑tax records [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)[[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14).  

7. **File the right forms and pay on time**  
   | Tax | Form(s) | Due dates | Notes | [Citation] |
   |------|--------|-----------|-------|-------------|
   | Income (earned as a sole proprietor, partner, or S‑corp shareholder) | 1040 S, 1040‑SE | 15 Oct next year (or due date of tax return) | Pay by 15 Oct if $1 000+ self‑employment tax is owed | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11) |

runs.question: do i need an ein and what accounting method comes with it
runs.answer:
**Do you need an EIN?**  
- An *Employer Identification Number (EIN)* is required if you:  
   • pay wages to one or more employees, or  
   • file pension or excise‑tax returns, or  
   • want a separate business tax identification number rather than using your Social‑Security # 【Segment 4】.  
- If you are a sole proprietor with **no employees** and have no other reason listed above, you can use your SSN for tax reporting, although many choose to obtain an EIN anyway for bank accounts and business‑related activities 【Segment 4】.  

**Which accounting method “comes with” an EIN?**  
- An EIN itself does **not** determine a specific accounting method.  
- When you file your first income‑tax return for the business (e.g., Schedule C for a sole proprietor), you must choose an accounting method that will be used for all future returns unless IRS approval is obtained to change it.  
- You can choose either the **cash method** or the **accrual method**:   
   • **Cash method** – income is reported when cash is actually received; expenses are deducted when paid 【Segment 5】.  
   • **Accrual method** – income is reported when earned, even if cash is received later; expenses are deducted when incurred 【Segment 5】.  
- If your business keeps an inventory, the IRS generally requires you to use the accrual method for purchases and sales, though small‑business taxpayers may elect a simplified treatment 【Segment 24】.  

**Summary**  
- Get an EIN if you meet the criteria above; otherwise you may use your SSN.  
- When you first file taxes, choose either the cash or accrual method; the choice is independent of whether you have an EIN.

runs.question: what forms do i keep for injuries and how long do i keep them
runs.answer:
The OSHA rules require employers to keep specific injury‑and‑illness records:

| Form | Purpose | Where it’s kept | Minimum retention period |
|------|---------|-----------------|--------------------------|
| **OSHA Form 300** – Log of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses | Records every recordable injury or illness (except minor first‑aid cases) | At the worksite (or in a system that meets OSHA’s electronic‑recordkeeping requirements) | **At least 5 years** from the date the record is made [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **OSHA Form 301** – Injury and Illness Incident Report | Detailed supplementary record for each recordable case | Same location as Form 300 | **At least 5 years** from the date the record is made [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **OSHA Form 300A** – Summary of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses | Yearly summary for use on OSHA reports and for internal management | Same location as Forms 300/301 | **At least 5 years** from the date the summary is prepared | **Additionally,** if your business has 100+ employees in a high‑hazard industry, you must electronically submit the 300/301 data to OSHA each year by March 2 of the following year [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14).

So, keep the OSHA Form 300 log, the OSHA Form 301 incident reports, and the OSHA Form 300A summary on file at the worksite (or in an approved electronic system) for at least five years.
